skills.name: Use a displacement-time graph to find period, frequency and amplitude

note.text:
A displacement-time graph shows how one particle moves as time passes.
• Amplitude a: the greatest displacement from the rest position, in metres (or cm). It is measured from the middle line to a crest, not from crest to trough.
• Period T: the time for one complete vibration, in seconds. On the graph it is the time from one crest to the next.
• Frequency f: the number of complete vibrations each second, in hertz (Hz).
f = 1/T and T = 1/f.
The energy a wave carries grows with its amplitude; a louder sound or a brighter light has a larger amplitude.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to read amplitude and period from a displacement-time graph and change between period and frequency.
Builds on: Lesson {8} (what a wave is) and Form Three measurement of time.
Leads to: Lesson {10}, where wavelength and the equation v = fλ are added.

sections.heading: Reading the graph
sections.text:
A displacement-time graph follows one particle as time passes. Time runs across; displacement from the rest position runs up and down.
• Amplitude a is the greatest displacement from the middle line. If the curve reaches {4} cm above and {4} cm below, the amplitude is {4} cm, not {8} cm.
• Period T is the time for one complete vibration: from one crest to the next crest, or from one trough to the next. If {2} complete waves take {0.4} s, then T = {0.2} s.
A bigger amplitude means the wave carries more energy: a louder sound, a brighter light, a taller sea wave.

sections.heading: Period and frequency
sections.text:
Frequency f is the number of complete vibrations each second, measured in hertz (Hz). One hertz is one vibration per second.
Period and frequency are reciprocals:
• f = {1} ÷ T  • T = {1} ÷ f
Examples:
• T = {0.2} s gives f = {1} ÷ {0.2} = {5} Hz.
• f = {50} Hz gives T = {1} ÷ {50} = {0.02} s.
If a particle makes {60} vibrations in {4} s, then f = {60} ÷ {4} = {15} Hz, and T = {1} ÷ {15} s.

key_words.meaning: the greatest displacement from the rest position
the time for one complete vibration, in seconds
how far a particle is from its rest position, and in which direction

examples: crest {3} cm above the line → amplitude {3} cm

mistake.wrong: amplitude = the height from a crest to a trough
mistake.right: amplitude = from the middle line to a crest
mistake.why: Crest to trough is twice the amplitude.

worked_example.problem: A displacement-time graph of a vibrating particle is shown. Find its amplitude, period and frequency.
steps: Amplitude: the greatest displacement from the middle line is {a} cm.
Period: one complete wave takes {T} s, read from one crest to the next.
worked_example.answer: amplitude {a} cm, period {T} s, frequency {waveT(T)} Hz

cards.idea: Amplitude is measured from the middle line to a crest, not from crest to trough.
example: a graph reaching {4} cm above and {4} cm below the line has amplitude {4} cm

cards.idea: The period is the time for one complete vibration; read it from crest to crest.
example: two complete waves in {0.4} s means T = {0.2} s

cards.idea: f = {1}/T and T = {1}/f; frequency is in hertz.

questions.prompt: From the displacement-time graph, what is the amplitude of the vibration, in cm?

misconceptions.explain: That is the distance from a crest to a trough: the amplitude is half of it.
{T} s is the period, read along the time axis.

solution: Amplitude is the greatest displacement from the middle line.
The graph reaches {a} cm above the line, so the amplitude is {answer} cm.

questions.prompt: From the graph, what is the period of the vibration, in seconds?

misconceptions.explain: {2 * T} s is the time for TWO complete waves; one takes half of it.
{a} cm is the amplitude, read up the displacement axis.

solution: The period is the time for one complete wave.
The graph shows {2} complete waves in {2 * T} s, so T = {answer} s.

questions.prompt: A vibration has a period of {T} s. Find its frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, not the period itself.
Divide {1} by the period; do not multiply.

questions.prompt: A tuning fork vibrates at {f} Hz. Find its period, in seconds.

misconceptions.explain: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency.
Frequency is counted per second, so divide {1} by it, not {60}.

questions.prompt: A particle makes {n} complete vibrations in {t} seconds. Find its frequency, in hertz.

misconceptions.explain: Divide the number of vibrations by the time, not the other way round.
That is the period, the time for ONE vibration.

solution: Frequency is the number of complete vibrations each second.
